blocks.text: Diner Kitsch is the Baby Boomer & Silent Generation revival of various 1940s-1950s cultural iconography, design, and kitsch associated with diner, drive-ins and malt shop culture.

It is characterized by the stylized re-use of mid-century American roadside dining imagery (neon signage, chrome accents, checkerboard floors, vinyl upholstery, jukeboxes, and other decorative elements) within later media, commercial spaces, and consumer goods that evoke a nostalgic, often idealized version of this era.

Diner Kitsch began in the mid-1970s, as part of the revival of 1950s aesthetics as people wanted to go back to an easier time away from the cultural climate. Restaurants and diners started to use 50s deco to appear kitschy and nostalgic.
Leather booths and deep vinyl in pastel or tones with channel-back tufting.
High-contrast white-and-black checkerboard floor tile patterns.
Polished chrome edges on bar stools, tables, and counter trims.
The color palette consists mint greens, hot pinks, bold reds, and turquoise paired with white and black.
